## Caption (verbatim)

```
The Rosary is not a soft prayer.
It's a battle cry that has echoed through 800 years of spiritual warfare — from the stone cells of medieval monasteries to the blood-soaked decks of Lepanto.
Most people don't know this: the Rosary was born because illiterate monks couldn't read the 150 Psalms. So they replaced each Psalm with a prayer — first the Our Father, then the Hail Mary. They used knotted cords, then wooden beads, to keep count. What started as the "poor man's psalter" became the most powerful devotion in the Church.
And every word of it is rooted in Scripture.
"Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee" — that's the Angel Gabriel, straight from Luke 1:28. "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb" — that's Elizabeth at the Visitation, Luke 1:42. The Our Father? Christ's own words from Matthew 6:9-13. The 20 mysteries? Each one is a meditation on a real event from the Gospels — the Annunciation, the Crucifixion, the Resurrection, the Descent of the Holy Spirit.
In 1571, the Ottoman fleet outnumbered Christendom's navy. Pope Pius V called all of Europe to pray the Rosary. On October 7, the Christian forces won the Battle of Lepanto — and the Pope established the Feast of the Holy Rosary to mark the victory.
This prayer has made empires kneel.
What makes you think it can't change your life?
Padre Pio prayed it daily. Mother Teresa called it her anchor. Pope John Paul II added five new mysteries in 2002 — the Luminous Mysteries — because he believed the Rosary was still revealing new depths of Christ's life to the faithful.
It's not decoration. It's not tradition for tradition's sake. It's a weapon forged in Scripture, tested in battle, and handed to you by the Queen of Heaven herself.
Pick it up.

"Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women."
— Luke 1:28, 1:42
```
